#5423. Tech companies are betting big on AI shopping, but Americans may already have bot fatigue as 72% don’t plan to use it for holiday gifts

Tech companies have spent the past year teaching AI how to shop. Google has introduced an AI-powered shopping cart, Meta’s Muse can search for products and prepare purchases for approval, and OpenAI’s new ChatGPT Wallet lets eligible users pay for purchases through an AI agent. Adobe expects traffic from AI tools to U.S. retail sites to jump 130% this holiday season.

Americans, it turns out, aren’t nearly as eager to hand over their gift lists.

Nearly three-quarters of Americans, or 72%, say they don’t plan to use AI tools for holiday shopping this year, up from 49% in 2025, according to a new Bank of America survey. The 23-percentage-point jump suggests a gap between the industry’s ambitions for AI shopping and what consumers say they want from it.

The reasons shoppers gave suggest that when it comes to gifts, efficiency isn’t the point. Among those who don’t plan to use the technology, 42% cited personal or ethical reasons, 37% said it takes away the personal aspect of gift giving, and 26% said they don’t trust AI recommendations.

Lora Monfared, head of consumer credit card products at Bank of America, said shoppers may be growing more selective about when AI is worth using, especially as they keep a closer eye on holiday spending.

“Some of last year’s curiosity about AI may also have worn off, and we could be seeing a bit of AI fatigue,” Monfared told Fortune. “Gift shopping is personal, and people want to feel good about what they’re giving.”

The survey found that 87% of Americans expect to spend the same amount or less on holiday shopping this year, while 63% said they base their spending strictly on their own budgets rather than what friends or family spend. Monfared said that same approach may be shaping how consumers use AI and social media to shop.

Colleen Kirk, a professor of marketing and management at New York Institute of Technology, said the hesitation may have less to do with what AI can do than what shoppers feel they lose by using it.

“Gift giving is a very personal act, and gifts, especially to close family and friends, are given from the heart,” Kirk told Fortune.

In her research studying consumer psychology, she has found that consumers can feel guilty when they use AI to write heartfelt messages because the words no longer feel entirely their own. She believes the same concern can extend to gift giving, where the time and thought spent choosing something for another person are part of what makes the gesture meaningful.

That effort creates what researchers call psychological ownership, or the feeling of having a personal stake in something. Kirk said browsing stores, comparing options online, and choosing a gift can make shoppers feel as though they’re giving part of themselves to someone else.

“Using AI can take away this sense of ownership,” she said. “It’s like the AI owns the process rather than me.”

That doesn’t mean shoppers are swearing off AI entirely—they’re just giving it the unglamorous jobs. The Bank of America survey found that 17% plan to use AI to compare prices or deals, 14% for gift ideas or inspiration, and 7% to write messages or cards. Respondents could select more than one use.

Bank of America said it asked the AI shopping question the same way in both years, though the survey only measures intentions, and those tend to get flexible in the last-minute scramble before Christmas. The bank doesn’t have data showing whether shoppers are actually using AI less.

Still, it’s an awkward moment for tech companies betting that shoppers will eventually trust AI to do more than recommend products, including making purchases on their behalf.

Kirk said AI may have a more natural place in the less personal parts of shopping, such as finding coupons, comparing prices, or buying groceries and household supplies. Those tasks can save consumers time and money without asking them to give up complete control over more meaningful purchases.

For gift shopping, she suggested consumers come up with their own ideas first, then turn to AI to help narrow their options. Research has found that people feel more ownership over an outcome when they generate their own ideas before using AI, she said.

And with holiday shopping competing for time that could be spent with family and friends, Kirk said some consumers may decide that letting AI handle the less personal tasks is a worthwhile trade-off.

“Consumers might just decide that it is worth it to give up a little bit of ownership of the process in exchange for getting more time for those special emotional connections with the humans they love,” Kirk said.

Tatiana Sataua is a News Fellow at Fortune covering business, technology, AI, and consumer culture.

#5422. Seattle VC firm Ascend closes $17M fund to back ‘Third Act’ startups in physical AI and hardware

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 7:15 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:30 am

Venture firm Ascend has closed a $17 million third fund and landed its first institutional investor, in what founder Kirby Winfield calls the toughest fundraising market for small venture firms in 15 years.

The Seattle-based firm invests at the earliest stage, often writing the first check into a startup. It was the first investor in Overland AI, the maker of autonomous military vehicles, and an early backer of subsea geothermal startup Endurance Energy, among others.

Ascend Fund III will back more physical AI startups building robots, energy systems, defense technology and other ventures that blend software and hardware — part of a larger bet on what the Ascend team likes to call Seattle’s “Third Act.”

Winfield said raising a third fund in this market shows that Ascend has “arrived on the national stage,” along with Seattle’s rise as a hub for this new class of startups. He said the firm’s track record puts it in the same league as the country’s top seed investors.

“We are not just some nice guys in the corner of the country helping out our neighbors,” said Winfield, who works closely with Jen Haller, Ascend partner and chief of staff, and Nate Bek, a principal at the firm.

Who’s backing the fund: The new institutional investor is FirstLook Partners, a firm that invests in smaller venture funds. Josh Porter, FirstLook’s co-founder and managing partner, said the firm, which is “very bullish on the Seattle ecosystem,” looked at several startup markets outside San Francisco and New York and met many investors in Seattle, “but all roads kept leading back to Kirby.”

Porter said Winfield has “lived the founder journey” and has “the operational chops to sit across the table from a founder and empathize with what they’re going through.”

The rest of the fund comes from family offices, founders who have sold companies, and more than a dozen founders of Ascend portfolio companies.

A tough market for small funds: Ascend’s raise comes as smaller venture firms struggle to bring in new money. Their investors, mostly wealthy individuals and family offices, are waiting longer for returns from earlier funds.

Just 211 newer venture firms closed at least one fund through the end of September, down from 927 in all of 2022, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. Established firms took a record 88.2% of the money raised by U.S. venture funds in the first nine months of the year, the report found. Porter said smaller firms have to show “a right to exist and a right to win deals.”

Ascend launched its first fund in 2019 and ultimately raised $15 million. Its second fund closed at $25 million in 2023. The firm generally operates in the $15 million to $25 million range and writes the same size checks regardless of fund size, Winfield said.

“We think Kirby knows his place in the larger ecosystem, knows the value he brings to the table, and has sized his fund accordingly,” Porter said.

The firm has already drawn about 60% of the money committed to Fund III. GeekWire first reported that the firm was raising the fund in April 2025, based on filings at the time. Endurance was one of the firm’s first investments from the new fund, in mid-2025.

Ascend’s track record: Winfield started Ascend after two decades in leadership roles at four startups. He described the first fund as a proof of concept that “stumbled into some unicorns,” including Fabric, an e-commerce software company that was valued at $1.5 billion in 2022. Ascend was in its first round.

With its second fund, Ascend moved away from consumer and marketplace investing to focus on enterprise AI and deep tech. Its most successful investments from that fund, according to Winfield, include Overland AI, Sabi, Yoodli and Zocks.

After Ascend’s first checks, its portfolio companies have gone on to raise more than $1.5 billion from investors including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer, Founders Fund, Khosla and Lightspeed, according to Ascend.

Ascend’s second and third funds rank in the top 10% of funds of $50 million or less, based on current valuations of their portfolio companies, Winfield said, citing figures Ascend shared with its investors at its annual meeting. The firm didn’t disclose specific returns or how much cash it has returned to its investors.

What Ascend looks for: The firm looks for ideas that seem too difficult, too boring, too confusing or too small for big multistage venture firms to evaluate. Ideally, Winfield said, its founders are doing something that makes Series A investors “a little bit nervous.”

That’s why Ascend hasn’t made many more defense tech investments since backing Overland, he said. Valuations for well-known founders in the sector have soared as more investors have piled in.

“The time to invest in defense tech was when nobody was investing in defense tech,” Winfield said.

Porter said Ascend’s focus on Seattle and physical AI is “really the bet we made with Ascend,” adding that Endurance and Overland have the potential to become “generational, category-defining companies.”

Fund III also backs AI software and infrastructure companies, including Seattle-area startup Govstream.ai, which uses AI to speed city permitting.

Seattle’s economic climate: Winfield is a champion of Seattle’s startup scene, known for Ascend’s annual Founders Bash party in the city and his ever-present ☔🔥☔ emojis on social media, symbolizing hot startups in rainy Seattle.

Ascend’s refreshed website and brand, launched with Fund III, nod to the firm’s Seattle roots with its longstanding Seattle Startup Toolkit and a Spotify playlist of Pacific Northwest indie rock and hip-hop.

But Winfield has also been a vocal critic of state and local policies he sees as hostile to startups, including Washington’s new tax on income over $1 million, which takes effect in 2028 and survived a repeal vote last week. He worries the tax could eventually be extended to people earning $150,000 a year, which would make it harder for startups to recruit employees from places like Texas.

“The chilling effect that’s going to have on the ecosystem is real, and it’s happening,” he said.

About 60% of Ascend’s portfolio companies are based in Seattle, according to the firm.

Bek said hardware companies such as Endurance and Overland still have good reasons to be in Seattle, including testing on Lake Union and in Yakima, access to the sea and University of Washington talent. For Overland, he said, that also means proximity to Joint Base Lewis-McChord.

Combined with the region’s history in aerospace, defense and energy, Winfield noted, those advantages make Seattle one of the country’s key hubs for building physical products. He called it “El Segundo Northwest,” a reference to the Los Angeles-area city that has become a hub for defense and hardware startups.

As Winfield notes, Ascend isn’t the only early-stage firm chasing these companies. Pre-seed firms such as Cantos, Ironspring and Silent Ventures are backing similar founders, and some Seattle firms that historically focused on software are becoming more open to investing in hardware.

Ultimately, he said, Seattle still benefits from a long legacy of technical founders, and Ascend is “betting that those folks are going to continue to create companies that are worth hundreds of billions of dollars.”

#5421. Bots in the boardroom: Could an AI ever replace board directors?

Board members are busy putting AI to work, using it to summarize lengthy papers, track market trends, and answer their questions. But some boards are going one step further and deploying AI in the boardroom.

Diligent makes software that directors use to share documents and run meetings. When its boss, Brian Strafford, told one chief executive about the company’s new board bot, their response hinted at where the technology may be headed. “I love the idea,” he said. “I’d immediately replace a couple of my board members with AI.” He then asked whether it could be priced at half what he pays his directors. “I want to make them nervous,” the CEO said.

The exchange, though spoken half in jest, raises a serious question: How far can, and should, AI go in the boardroom? While many executives remain hesitant about using AI in this setting, others are experimenting with creating digital replicas of colleagues to rehearse potentially difficult boardroom discussions, according to Stafford.

In April, Lloyds Banking Group became the first FTSE 100 firm to acknowledge it deploys an AI agent to support boardroom activities, The Times reported. Its executives and directors reportedly use the bot for agenda planning and analysis before high-level meetings, and to help mitigate human bias.

Pippa Begg, chief executive of Board Intelligence, which builds AI software for boards, says that AI could eventually sit in on meetings and be “able to almost interrupt and say: ‘Hang on, I think you’re falling into this trap.’ Or: ‘I disagree.’” However, giving it a formal legal vote, she added, would be “a dangerous leap.”

AI brings clear advantages to the boardroom, says Joanne McEnteggart, global head of debt, capital markets, and corporate at IQ-EQ, a fund-services firm that administers around 30,000 board meetings a year across 25 countries. “AI can assimilate information quickly and dissect years of data,” she says. “It removes emotion, stress, and bias, and can call out a director who seems to be deciding against the facts.”

Some boards have reportedly used it to break a stalemate during discussions, a role usually played by the chair, McEnteggart adds.

For now, she notes, it mostly summarizes board papers and tidies up minutes. But even that is changing how directors prepare. One director she has known for years has started asking questions they never would have before. “That’s good,” she says, “because it challenges thought.”

“I’d immediately replace a couple of my board members with AI.”

One place Stafford sees AI playing a big role is reducing boards’ reliance on external advisors, with AI specialists filling gaps in directors’ knowledge. “Clients are asking for a Middle East expert, a sustainability expert, a futurist,” he says.

One chief executive uses AI to play the role of an activist investor to provide a dissenting voice. At one acquisitive company, a director asks the AI to argue against every deal. With no one around the table having to play devil’s advocate, Stafford says boards can avoid “awkward” arguments.

Not everyone is convinced. There is a risk AI could become a new source of boardroom groupthink if directors lean too heavily on a tool few fully understand, says Mark Freebairn, head of the board practice at search firm Odgers. “I sometimes feel like I’m the only person that’s seen Terminator 2,” he says.

People think that AI is impartial and makes decisions with “zero emotion, zero human risk of bias,” he says. “How can you test what an algorithm tells you is right? That feels like one hell of a risk.”

As AI’s role shifts from notetaker to sparring partner, boards are deciding where to draw the line. Nearly half (49%) of directors say their board is actively reviewing which decisions should continue to be made by humans as the capabilities of AI improve, according to a survey of more than 400 directors, CEOs and CFOs by Board Intelligence.

However AI is used, it cannot take on a director’s legal responsibilities. McEnteggart says: “A bot cannot be held personally responsible in law nor can anyone vouch that it is fit and proper to sit on a board.”

Freebairn is aware of boards that have given a bot a seat and a vote, though it remains “very uncommon.” Doing so, he says, means “accepting a robot adds as much value as a human”.

Kazakhstan’s sovereign wealth fund, Samruk-Kazyna, appointed an AI board member called SKAI and gave it voting rights last year. Its chief executive says SKAI “voted on all the items” at its first meeting, but the country’s financial regulator says the appointment breaches national law. SKAI remains on the board as a pilot, according to a recent filing.

“A bot cannot be held personally responsible in law.”

Abu Dhabi’s International Holding Company, the UAE’s largest listed firm, gave a non-voting seat on its board to an AI called Aiden Insight. The AI has issued statements in its name, in which it describes itself as “a C-level AI entity.”

Deanna Strable, chief executive of Principal Financial Group, who also sits on the board of health insurer Elevance Health, doubts this will become mainstream, though she will not rule it out. “My gut answer would be no. But so much has happened in the past year.” If it does happen, she expects AI’s vote to be advisory rather than decisive.

A lack of guidance on how directors should use AI represents another risk. Half of U.S. public companies lack a board-specific AI policy and only 14% have given directors company-approved AI tools for board work, according to a survey by Deloitte and the Society for Corporate Governance.

Board papers are among the most sensitive documents a company holds, routinely containing unannounced deals, unpublished results, and succession plans. Many directors are retired executives without access to enterprise AI tools, Stafford notes, so they fall back on consumer chatbots that offer weaker data protection. Upload them to ChatGPT, Stafford warns, and it will have them “forever.” Boards need to be clear on “what company data is going where,” McEnteggart adds.

Two-thirds of directors and executives say their boards have limited or no knowledge of AI, according to a separate 2025 Deloitte survey of nearly 700 respondents in 56 countries. “Most board members do not understand the complexity of rolling this out,” Strable says.

Seven in ten large European companies now have defined board oversight of AI, according to proxy advisor Glass Lewis, but that covers how companies use AI, not how directors themselves do.

As AI is used more frequently to inform board decisions, the role of directors risks changing. “If you take humans out of judgment,” Freebairn says, “there’s nothing else we offer really.”

Research suggests judgment and trust are where humans still have the edge. In a test by Wharton and INSEAD researchers, a board of AI chatbots outperformed six human boards on decision quality and use of evidence, but it struggled to build trust. The researchers concluded that AI is better used to stress-test a board’s thinking than to replace it.

Even the CEO selling a board bot urges restraint. “AI slop is a big issue, so you don’t want that creeping its way into the boardroom,” Stafford says. “More is not always better. It is just more.”

Sam Birchall is a features writer at Fortune 500 C-Suite Europe. Previously, she was a reporter at Raconteur, where she specialized in business and leadership storytelling for C-suite audiences.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:24 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:04 am

— Dan Ayoub, the past head of Dungeons & Dragons, has been named president of Wizards of the Coast & Hasbro Digital Games. Ayoub joined the Renton, Wash.-based Wizards of the Coast in 2022 and counts himself among the longtime players of D&D and Magic: The Gathering.

“D&D is 52 years old. Magic is 33. Brands don’t last that long because of any one leader; they last because generations of creators and fans keep choosing them,” Ayoub said. “We owe it to them to protect what makes these worlds special.”

Paramount Skydance last month completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), with the combined company taking the name Skydance. Shortly after, the company announced the departure of two WBD leaders from the Bellevue site: Avi Saxena and Tyler Whitworth.

He left in 2021 to become CEO of Archenia, a Las Vegas-based customer qualification and acquisition company, which Marchex acquired in July.

Troy Hartless, who in September 2025 added president to his role as chief revenue officer, will return to serving solely as CRO.

Janashvili joins from Surami Partners, which provides financial services for clean tech companies, and previously led climate tech investment banking at CIBC Capital Markets. Across numerous roles, he has advised boards and management teams of public and soon-to-be public companies.

“Her appointment as Chairman recognizes more than a decade of leadership at Gravity and her role in helping the company grow while remaining focused on the independent businesses and employees it serves,” the company said.

#5419. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5418. Jensen Huang’s $145 billion question: What California divorce law says Lori Huang could get

Jensen Huang has lost his job, his board seat, and roughly $10 billion in paper wealth since admitting to an affair. If his 41-year marriage ends, California law could put a far larger share of his fortune in play.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s president, CEO, and director this week, days after confessing in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had been unfaithful to Lori Huang, his wife since 1985. The board named chief financial officer Colette Kress Nvidia’s interim CEO and made longtime director Harvey Jones its first board chair while it searches for a permanent successor.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang wrote.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The admission followed a New York Times report that U.S. intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, of gathering information for Beijing, and that she had a close relationship with Huang. China has denied involvement. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said this week that she left Singapore in February and was barred from returning after a police investigation, which it said “did not concern espionage.”

Two more relationships have since been reported. The New York Times reported on November 11 that Huang had been romantically involved with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported directly to him, citing five people who had worked at the company. A day later, Reuters reported that Huang had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee, whom it did not name. Powell did not respond to the Times, and Nvidia declined to comment to Reuters.

Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort and said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” An FBI inquiry into his relationship with Alice Huang is also underway.

Huang has not announced plans to divorce. But a split would test how California divides a fortune built almost entirely on a single stock, and the answer would turn less on his headline net worth than on how the couple’s Nvidia shares were acquired and held.

Huang reported beneficial ownership of about 870.6 million Nvidia shares, or 3.58% of the company’s outstanding stock, as of March 23, 2026, according to Nvidia’s 2026 proxy statement. Nvidia ranked No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and was the first company on the list worth more than $4 trillion.

Jensen and Lori Huang are co-trustees of their living trust, which holds about 528.5 million shares, and of two other family trusts. Together, the three trusts hold nearly 669 million shares. Another 73.3 million shares are held by limited liability companies whose sole member is the living trust.

Lori Huang also runs the family’s philanthropy. She is president of the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, which reported about $9.2 billion in assets at the end of 2024, Fortune reported. The foundation holds about 58.7 million Nvidia shares, but the proxy states that neither spouse has a pecuniary interest in them.

The distinction matters. Beneficial ownership and control of shares do not by themselves establish personal ownership, or determine how assets would be divided in a divorce.

The couple met as lab partners at Oregon State University and married in 1985, eight years before Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993. They live in California, a community-property state, where assets acquired during a marriage are generally owned jointly and divided equally in a divorce.

“In California, all property acquired by a spouse during marriage is community property,” Christopher Melcher, a Los Angeles attorney who specializes in high-net-worth divorces, told the New York Post. “She would be entitled to 50%.”

Under California Courts guidance, community property generally includes earnings and assets acquired between the date of marriage and the date of separation. Property owned before the marriage or acquired after separation, along with gifts and inheritances, is generally separate property, and some assets can be a mix of both.

That means Lori Huang could be entitled to half of the community-property portion of the couple’s Nvidia holdings, not necessarily half of every share tied to her husband.

The outcome would depend on how the shares were acquired, how the trusts are structured, whether separate and community assets were mixed, and whether the couple signed a prenuptial or postnuptial agreement. A court would need to examine those details before deciding what either spouse receives.

California is also a no-fault divorce state, meaning either spouse can seek a divorce without proving infidelity or other wrongdoing. Infidelity, even across several reported relationships, generally does not entitle one spouse to a larger share of community property.

Huang is worth about $145 billion and ranks as the world’s 13th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, as Fortune reported. That figure is a market estimate, not a tally of marital property, and it rises and falls with Nvidia’s stock, which shed $450 billion in market value in the days after his admission.

Huang has described his wife’s role in the company in plain terms. “Every moment of Nvidia, she was there,” he said in an interview with CNA.

#5417. AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:51 am

AWS says its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the company is touting that as a selling point.

AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine. It’s built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. Developers and AI coding agents can use it to test code without a network connection and without paying for the real cloud.

The tool addresses a problem that coding agents such as Amazon’s Kiro and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made worse. Agents can write code faster than teams can test it against the real cloud. Agents check their work by running the code and reading the results, over and over, and doing that in the cloud adds delays and costs.

The emulator lets them run that loop on a developer’s own machine.

In an ironic or perhaps appropriate twist, AWS used AI agents to build the emulator. Agents also maintain it, testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find.

“The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” wrote Matt Goldberg, the AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, in a blog post.

Goldberg compared his agents to himself as a kindergartner, too young to hold a crayon properly, who got yelled at by classmates for ruining a group drawing of dinosaurs. The problem wasn’t bad intent, he wrote, just a lack of competence. The answer, for agents, is clearly defined areas to fill in.

“I think agents also need coloring books,” he wrote.

The agents work from AWS’s public API models, which describe how each service should behave, and check their work against the real AWS cloud.

The agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. One writes “fidelity tests” — real-world scenarios such as creating a queue, sending a message and deleting the queue — and checks each against real AWS. A second runs those tests against the emulator and files issues for failures, and a third fixes them, one agent per issue.

Every change passes through an automated gate where other agents check coding standards and security. Goldberg wrote that hundreds of agents now fix thousands of issues a day.

The project started as a weekend experiment, inspired by Anthropic’s demonstration earlier this year in which a team of Claude agents built a C compiler. Goldberg gave Kiro a three-step prompt and got a passable first version of Amazon SQS, AWS’s message queuing service, in 15 minutes.

By the end of the weekend, Goldberg wrote, Kiro had built a rough version of the rest of AWS, with obvious gaps, and his team started using it to test its software that Monday.

Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI and emerging tech, tied the project to a lesson he described to GeekWire in June. He spent four nights babysitting Kiro as it tried to rebuild a replication engine he and Allan Vermeulen built by hand nearly 20 years ago.

Once he gave the agent a spec and a way to test its work, the job took about two hours.

“When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct,” Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on CTO Werner Vogels’ blog.

It’s the same idea behind Amazon’s recent move to rewrite its engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code.

The emulator has limits. Devin Pratt, an IDC analyst, told InfoWorld that it doesn’t yet simulate throttling, outages or differences in which services and features are available by region, and that it doesn’t sandbox the code it runs. The agents’ backlog of known gaps is public, in a GitHub folder called “things-that-do-not-work.”

Other AWS emulators exist, most notably LocalStack, which this year put its free version behind an account requirement and limited it to noncommercial use. AWS released its emulator for free under CC0, a public domain dedication, with the full commit history on GitHub.

The company says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

#5416. Meet ‘Captain Keel,’ the 37-year-old steering a Bitcoin miner into the AI data center gold rush

In late 2023, Bitcoin miner Ben Gagnon concluded that his employer, Bitfarms of Quebec, was in the wrong business. For Gagnon, Bitfarms’ greatest value lay not in the giant racks of GPUs that generated Bitcoin, but the immense power supplies it controlled. The then 34-year-old chief mining officer who’d launched his career crafting makeshift crypto-minting rigs in Hong Kong and Taipei, reckoned that Bitfarms could make much more money by exiting the field full stop, demolishing the “mines,” selling the chips that filled them, and re-channeling its plentiful flow of megawatts to power-craving industrial users at plants newly built on the Bitfarms sites.

The big revelation came in March of 2024, when Core Scientific and CoreWeave unveiled a stunning new deal. Bitcoin titan Core Scientific would refashion a mining facility in Austin, Texas, as an AI data center, and rent the power and buildings to the neocloud. That Bitcoin-to-AI play struck Gagnon as a model that Bitfarms could follow on a grand scale, from Quebec to Washington state. “It was the big aha moment,” recalls Gagnon. “Suddenly, we saw who the right customer was.”

At the time, Bitfarms was mired in turmoil. In early 2024, the board was searching for its third leader in five years. The sitting chief agreed to depart when Bitfarms named a successor, but in May—believe it or not while still CEO—instead filed a $27 million suit for “wrongful termination and breach of contract,” plunging this Canadian exemplar of all-green, hydro-driven Bitcoin mining into legal warfare. Pounded by a sharp drop in the token’s prices, Bitfarms’ stock was languishing, and a rival pounced. Two days after the board fired the CEO, Riot Platforms unveiled a hostile $930 million takeover bid for Bitfarms at a lowly $2.30 a share, 75% below its peak in late 2021. After Bitfarms installed a “poison pill” defense, Riot launched a website dubbed “A Better Bitfarms” trashing allegedly poor corporate governance, and demanding the departure of the co-founder named as interim chief.

The board tapped Gagnon to both quell the war versus Riot, and pursue the strategy of total transformation he’d been advocating. In July of 2024, Gagnon took the helm, and over the next few months, helped broker an agreement where Riot named a director of its choice, and the co-founder left the board. Riot halted its attack and has since sold its shares.

While battling for Bitfarms’ independence, Gagnon kept his sights locked on engineering the Big Pivot. He describes the mission as “pursuing a strategy of steering the business away from Bitcoin mining, and taking it over to a pure energy infrastructure play in support of AI and high-performance computing. We’d shift our focus entirely to addressing the defining constraint of the most important technology of our lifetime.”

The venture needed a rebrand, so Gagnon picked “Keel” to evoke the structural backbone of a vessel that, as he says, “provides stability and converts energy into forward motion,” a reference to the stable long-term leases that he expects to provide a smooth and lucrative course versus the storms he encountered in Bitcoin. He’s now attempting to pull a hat trick seldom seen in the corporate world, the total reinvention of a large enterprise, including in product and nationality, on a crazy-rhythm beat. On April 1, 2026, the franchise was reborn as Keel Infrastructure and changed its domicile from Canada to the U.S. The photo on Gagnon’s X profile reprises the nautical theme, adding a whimsical accent. Gagnon grins from a porthole-sized frame, sporting his usual oversized rimless glasses, and a gold-braided yachtsman’s cap displaying his user name, “Captain Keel.”

Now 37, Gagnon is making by far his biggest wager yet in a career that careened from mining Bitcoin in remote oil patches by rescuing flared natural gas to rehabilitating some of the world’s dirtiest energy sites under the banner of AI.

Gagnon is the son of two American parents who settled in Hong Kong, where he attended international grammar and high schools that offered lots of, as he puts it, “Mandarin as a second language courses.” He gained a bachelor’s degree in business and economics (and a minor in Mandarin) at the Indiana University’s Kelley School of Business in 2011, on the Bloomington campus. “I got fascinated by Bitcoin, and could have bought it for 73 cents,” he recalls. “Instead, I did what every college kid does. I bought beer.” Over the next three-and-a-half years, he reflected on that choice while watching Bitcoin climb 1,400-fold to over $1,000.

Returning home, he attained a master’s in computer security and networking at the University of Hong Kong, where he took cryptography courses that renewed his interest in the science of generating cryptocurrencies. After graduating, Gagnon worked as a network technician at a company that offered mobile applications for investor conferences and other events. After less than two years, he quit his job and moved again, this time to Taiwan. His new venture: Building and running a jerry-rigged Ethereum mine at the home of his girlfriend’s (now his wife’s) parents in Taipei. “Everyone thought it was Bitcoin 2.0, so I figured, I’m not going to miss this opportunity like I missed Bitcoin as a sophomore,” says Gagnon.

The business drew unwanted attention by using ten times the electricity of a typical home in Taipei—specifically, the phenomenon alerted the police. “They couldn’t figure out what we were doing,” he recalls. “They thought we were growing marijuana upstairs and kept raiding the house, like on a weekly basis. So we had to explain to the police every week that we weren’t doing anything illegal.” It took only a couple of intolerable months before Gagnon saw the necessity of uprooting his facility from his future in-laws’ home.

Gagnon then ran his operation in Guangzhou on China’s mainland, but shut down after two years due to a tough regulatory climate. “Let’s just say that the laws were somewhat selective for a young foreigner navigating a new industry,” he avows. In 2019, he joined Bitfarms, one of several Bitcoin miners, including HIVE, that sprouted in Quebec during the 2017 to 2018 boom, drawn by the province’s plentiful and relatively inexpensive hydroelectric power. As chief of development, his charge was expanding the business to the U.S. and other energy-rich areas of Canada.

Gagnon focused on the huge but remote Alberta oil patch. “I was always looking for the cheapest energy sources for mining, and that was Alberta,” he says. The producers were “flaring” the natural gas created from drilling, since no pipelines existed for sending it to population centers. Gagnon created the first containerized Bitcoin data center that incorporated a generator and offered 100% financing. His mobile units channeled natural gas right at the far-flung drilling sites for minting tokens. His rigs empowered the drillers to monetize energy they were burning into the atmosphere. The product proved a big winner for his new employer. “The drillers were using gas that cost 1.5 cents a kWh versus 6 cents in the U.S.,” he recalls. “So we got great prices for our equipment because the payback period for the drillers was so short.”

When Gagnon started pushing the AI remake in 2023, he doubled-down on a possible acquisition that ideally fitted the new plotline. His target was Stronghold Digital, a startup using one of the most unusual models in all of Bitcoin mining. From the mid-19th century to the 1970s, mines in Pennsylvania routinely separated the low-quality coal—scraps mixed with rocks, often with high sulfur or ash content—from the good stuff. Children called “breaker boys” seated at conveyor belts or chutes would pick out the slate and rock by hand, no gloves permitted—brutal work that often left their fingers bleeding. The legacy: Black carbon mountains scarring the towns of western Pennsylvania. For decades, the sites Stronghold owned had been performing a public service by scooping truckloads of waste coal and burning it in their boilers to supply electricity to the local grids, while pocketing big subsidies for the effort. The state government reasoned that the benefits of cleansing the countryside more than compensated for allowing just about the dirtiest form of electrical generation in America.

In 2021, a pair of entrepreneurs turned those locations into Bitcoin mining operations. But Stronghold way overinvested in chips and other equipment, and by 2023 it was foundering, hammered by crippling debt and legal disputes. Gagnon identified Stronghold’s sweet spots, one each in eastern and western Pennsylvania, as ideal locations for AI campuses. Stronghold already controlled significant amounts of power, but held the potential to obtain much more. Working with its owners, Gagnon applied to utilities and state authorities for big new batches of megawatts. Once assured the approvals were at hand, Gagnon, in August 2024, after a month as CEO, landed an agreement to purchase Stronghold for $175 million.

Increasingly, AI leaders are viewing power as the toughest chokepoint in the AI supply chain. As OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman characterizes the issue, “The bottleneck for AI isn’t code, it’s electrons.” Adds Elon Musk, “The limiting factor is fundamentally electrical power…[that’s leading to] producing more chips than the hyperscalers can plug in and turn on.” And Greg Abel, CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, a major energy provider to AI data centers via its sundry utilities, concurs, calling access to megawatts a “big constraint” for rapid buildouts.

The backlash against AI data centers gained fresh force on Election Day, when so many candidates seeking restraints or outright bans on their spread won congressional and statewide races. That result may actually strengthen the hand of the Bitcoin contingent, since they’ve already got a grip on the energy pipelines the hyperscalers and neoclouds need, and appear willing to pay up for. Put simply, the future “scarcity value” of the crucial asset these crypto producers control likely jumped on November 3. Gagnon calls Keel’s position “bird in the hand economics.”

Keel stands among the first and largest crypto operators to follow Core Scientific into AI. But today, more than ten major players are making the switch, in part or whole. Among those that have already secured big, long-term contracts are Riot, which clinched a $9.1 billion lease from Anthropic for the AI campus at its Bitcoin mine in Milam County, Texas; Hut 8, partnering on a $7 billion contract with Google and Anthropic at its River Bend complex in Louisiana; and Applied Digital, which will serve CoreWeave under an $11 billion agreement at its forthcoming campus in Ellendale, North Dakota.

All of these converts are essentially re-purposing the same land and power, or sometimes more of the latter, that they deployed to produce Bitcoin for the AI buildout. But they’re taking different approaches. The crypto-to-AI crowd falls into two categories, both in how completely they’re shifting, and the templates they embrace. On the first score, several participants are taking the Keel route by totally exiting Bitcoin for AI, including Core Scientific, Cipher Mining and Genesis Digital. Another group that encompasses Riot, Hut 8, HIVE Digital Technologies, and TeraWulf are adopting a hybrid model where they both channel power to AI campuses and continue to mine Bitcoin.

On the second criterion, the two main business models are “compute provider” and “developer” or co-location (co-lo) purveyor. As a compute provider, the former or hybrid Bitcoin outfit delivers a turnkey project. It commissions a contractor, often a REIT, to erect the buildings, and typically rents the structures long-term from the builder-partner. It then packs the cavernous boxes with GPUs and other gear that constitute by far the most expensive part of the project. The owner’s product is the full computing package that it then leases to the hyperscalers or neoclouds for running the likes of Google’s Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude.

The developer or co-lo arrangement works much the same way, except that the site’s owner doesn’t supply the hardware, and hence shoulders much lower up-front costs. Instead, it’s the hyperscaler or neocloud, a Microsoft or Crusoe, that brings the GPUs and other equipment. The company branching out from Bitcoin mining both supplies the structures that it leases from the REIT or other contractor, and the power that runs it––MWs secured on long-term utility contracts form its essential business. The still-active or former Bitcoin miner rents the “powered shells” to the compute providers, for operating, say OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Microsoft’s Copilot. In today’s market, the developer garners a big markup on the scarcest item in AI.

The reasons so many are crossing from Bitcoin to follow either one or both of these strategies: Each megawatt of power at work generates far more cash flow at an AI campus than at plants churning codes to win the signature crypto coin. In a recent interview on the Schwab Network, Christian Lopez, head of blockchain and digital assets at broker-dealer Cohen & Co., estimates the numbers, over five years, at $1.7 million per KW for Bitcoin and almost five times as much, $7.9 million, for an AI campus. What about revenues? Sarah Friar, CFO of OpenAI, posits that each 1 GW (1,000 MW) fueling an AI data center garners $10 billion in revenues. Once again, the number can be one-fifth that amount for a Bitcoin mine.

Data center pioneers divide into two camps. The “compute” competitors (Bitdeer of Singapore, IREN of Australia and Canada’s HIVE Digital, Hut 8 to some degree) spend massively to buy the chips and rent them out, in exchange for higher rents, shorter leases, and more risk. For example, HIVE has a $350 million, 5-year deal with an as yet unnamed AI stalwart for campuses on Bell Canada sites where it’s supplying the hardware. “The cost of the GPUs is $190 million off the bat,” says HIVE CEO Aydin Kilic, who predicts the project will be multiple times as profitable per KW as Bitcoin mining.

By contrast, Keel is a pure-play developer. It doesn’t buy and install the GPUs and other gear that constitute as much as 70% of data centers that cost roughly $50 billion a GW to create (the other 30% covers land, the buildings and costs of connecting or providing onsite power). “We’re strictly in the power business, and make money on the difference between what we pay the utilities, and what the compute providers pay us on their leases,” says Gagnon.

Keel’s edge: It sits on an enormous amount of power. It has 2.2 GWs that are either approved for use, or in the last stages of the approval process. That’s more than the 1.9 GW that OpenAI was reportedly marshaling at the close of 2025. Gagnon acknowledges that Keel as a developer won’t collect revenues nearly as large as the miners turned compute providers, but insists that his cash flows will be more secure, and that the relatively low cost of the power and physical centers as a share of the whole makes customers willing to pay big premiums to get MWs in a hurry.

In part, that’s because as of now, those AI campuses are sumptuously profitable. “The gross margins for data centers are 85%, and of the 15% in costs, only a max of 2% to 4% goes to leasing the power and buildings,” Gagnon explains. “So if a customer spends twice as much, their margins may ease to 81% or 83%. The GPUs in their warehouses are depreciating fast. So they’re saying, I’d rather take a hit to 83% in gross margin and start generating revenue in 6 months than wait 12 months for a margin that’s 2 points higher. And that’s what we’re seeing.”

Keel is shepherding three “priority projects” closest to clearing all hurdles and to signing leases. One of them is a former Stronghold facility: Panther Creek, 85 miles north of Philadelphia. Keel acquired another Pennsylvania site in a separate transaction. It’s located at the opposite end of the state in Sharon, near Youngstown, Ohio. On the two sites combined, Keel’s in the process of securing over 450 MWs from the local grids. The third “priority” is a hydro project in Moses Lake, Washington, ringed by Seattle, Spokane and Portland. Gagnon marvels at the sight of the famous Boeing repair field almost adjoining the Keel site. “You’re driving to our facility and you’ll see 100 different 737 MAX, all painted different colors, what a fun sight!”

Gagnon points out that approvals fall into three categories: zoning, environmental, and development. At Moses Lake, Keel’s scored all three, and the site’s now under construction. At Sharon and Panther Creek, it has secured both zoning and development, and is working through the environmental permits, the final step. The most difficult requirement, he states, is zoning. “It’s the one that’s most political, most community-centric, and most emotional,” he says. “Projects can get shut down if you don’t behave the right way with community leaders. We got really good at advocating for Bitcoin mines that are a much harder sell than AI campuses.”

The second ex-Stronghold site is the biggest of them all, the 700-acre Scrubgrass facility near Sharon, and roughly an hour north of Pittsburgh. There, Keel’s applied for a massive 1 GW of power, 40% of the total capacity it’s seeking. At Scrubgrass, Keel is still working through all the initial permitting stages for securing power.

Gagnon says the biggest challenge isn’t attracting customers, it’s getting the final environmental permits in place. But he’s already encountered delays. In May, Gagnon guided to obtaining leases at all three priority projects by the end of 2026. But on the Q3 earnings call, he said that no deals will be signed this year, and declined to give dates for signing customers on those projects.

The rub: Keel’s now generating puny revenues since it’s now left Bitcoin mining and isn’t yet making money from AI. Gagnon’s sitting on a big cushion, having raised almost $600 million in convertible debt last year, and another almost $300 million by emptying its Bitcoin trove. Still, Keel’s burning cash fast. Will its trove prove big enough to fund crossing the span to AI on time? Investors are cautious about Keel’s prospects, to put it mildly. Keel’s stock dropped around 20% on Gagnon’s announcement of no deals this year, and currently has a paltry market cap of around $1.3 billion, about the same as when Riot bid back in 2024.

On the plus side, Gagnon’s collected a portfolio that potentially features some of the best AI sites in America and Canada. He notes that the big customers are now showing a strong preference for facilities near big population centers, just where he’s concentrating. “The difference is that until now, there’s been so much AI model training that wasn’t for customers, so it didn’t matter where the campus was located. The normal things that would have guided a developer to find a project and select a piece of land were thrown out the window in the interest of scale and time.”

Now, he says, the business is moving strongly towards “inference” where the compute providers sell to banks, research labs, call centers and other customers. “That’s where most of the money will be made, not on the retail side,” he says. “As the market moves to inference, more and more of the traditional data center qualities will come into play.” He notes that compute works much more efficiently when it’s near the customer than hundreds or thousands of miles away in a remote rural area. “It’s so important to get the fiber close to where people live and businesses are located, and in the frenzy, that’s been forgotten,” says Gagnon. The big distances cause sluggish responses that lead to poor user experiences in fields such as autonomous driving and interactive chatbots. Plus, he says, in the weeks leading up to and following the midterms, “we’ve seen a big uptick in level of demand and prioritization of our sites in Pennsylvania, driven that the support of data center had changed in many states. The Democratic candidates who won in Pennsylvania ran on platform favoring responsible data center development, the opposite the scenario in most other states.”

“The differentiator will be location, location and location,” says Gagnon. “This is a real estate industry and location is hugely important in real estate. That’s why you have so many cloud data centers in Loudoun County, Va. near D.C. and Quincy near Seattle. We’re near New York, Philly, and Pittsburgh, and have a great position in the Pacific Northwest, where there’s a big shortage of AI campuses. If you’re close to where the demand comes from, that should justify a premium going forward, just as it has in the past for data centers.”

Gagnon is especially bullish on the union of AI and the Keystone State. “Pennsylvania built this country, it had all the resources needed to launch the industrial revolution, steel, coal, railroads, natural gas. Texas was the first mover in AI data centers, and now Pennsylvania is the second mover. And we’ll be number one in Pennsylvania.”

It’s a long way from waste coal to GPUs. And Gagnon’s got a plausible story: The big guys have the GPUs, in fact too many of them. But he and his Bitcoin brethren have a lot of what the giants now need most, the power. The question for Keel is how fast Gagnon can turn it on.

Shawn Tully is a senior editor-at-large at Fortune, covering the biggest trends in business, aviation, politics, and leadership.

#5415. This Overlooked Career Is the First Step to a $200,000 Salary

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

This job faces a huge talent shortage, causing a spike in salaries.

Millennials wrote off tax accounting. Now Gen Z has a reason to give it a second look, as six-figure earnings and a talent shortage have resulted in a spike in salaries for tax experts.

Tax work has earned two spots on Monster’s seasonal jobs list. The company’s 2026 Seasonal Hiring Index names tax associates and tax experts among 13 titles that saw significant seasonal posting activity in 2025. The primary busy season for tax accountants runs from late January through April 15, spurred by individual and corporate tax deadlines.

“Seasonal work is more than a short-term paycheck; it’s often the start of a longer career journey,” the Monster report said. It added that many companies use seasonal roles as a testing ground for permanent ones.

According to ZipRecruiter, the average salary for U.S. tax associates is $33.40 an hour. The same site states that tax experts make $45.67 an hour in the U.S.

Tax jobs face a significant talent shortage, which is creating an opening for newcomers. The U.S. faced a shortage of 340,000 tax accountants in 2024, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, and employers are still struggling to recruit.

Companies surveyed by Personiv, a global finance and accounting outsourcing company, reported an average of 17 unfilled accounting and finance positions in 2026, compared with five a year earlier.

For job seekers, a seasonal tax role could lead to more opportunities than a temporary paycheck. It could be the first move toward a full-time career with six-figure earning potential, Fortune reports.

The catch with tax accounting is that the seasonal hiring rush may already be passing.

Anyone waiting until the holidays to start applying for seasonal tax roles risks missing the prime recruiting window.

Monster’s analysis found that seasonal job postings rose 44% between August and September last year, and peaked in October. By November, posting activity fell 24% from October. That indicates that the prime hiring time for these roles may have already passed.

Also, the bigger paychecks in accounting come with a higher bar to entry. Tax accountants typically need at least a bachelor’s degree. Meanwhile, earning a certified public accountant (CPA) license can open the door to better-paid roles, but requires an extensive investment of time and money. CPAs provide a range of services, including tax preparation and financial planning.

Investopedia reported total compensation of up to $200,000 for CPAs with four years of experience under their belt.

For young people looking for work, even a temporary position could offer a paycheck and experience. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, only 53.8% of young people (ages 16 to 24) were employed in July. The youth unemployment rate was 9.1% that month.

Additionally, the transition from college to the workforce has become more difficult. A survey from career services site Kickresume found that just 12% of recent graduates secured full-time jobs before graduation this year, compared with nearly 40% of earlier graduates.

AI is adding to that uncertainty. Goodwill CEO Steve Preston said in an interview with Fortune last year that automation is reducing entry-level opportunities, which are the jobs where young workers traditionally gain experience.

Seasonal openings aren’t always labeled that way.

In 2025, fewer than 3% of seasonal job postings included “seasonal,” “holiday,” or “temporary” in the title, per Monster. Searching for a specific role, such as “tax associate,” could uncover opportunities that a search for “holiday jobs” misses.

Monster also recommends widening the search across roles and industries.

“A seasonal opening can be hiding among jobs that, by title alone, look like ordinary year-round positions,” the report indicated.

#5414. Rand Fishkin’s Seattle game studio serves up first trailer for ‘The Snackbar at the End of the World’

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 11, 2026 at 11:21 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:21 am

If the eventual release of “The Snackbar at the End of the World” is a full-on meal for video game fans, news this week of the game’s first trailer should at least suffice as an appetizer.

Seattle-based Snackbar Studio, co-founded by SparkToro founder Rand Fishkin and his wife, writer Geraldine DeRuiter, unveiled its debut title and Steam page on Tuesday. The hand-drawn narrative adventure RPG puts players in the role of a chef trying to save a struggling family restaurant in a magical version of 1960s Italy.

The studio now plans to launch the game late next year, after originally targeting the second half of 2026. Snackbar raised $2.15 million from 38 angel investors two years ago, and the project began four years ago, according to Fishkin. The team includes five co-founders (Fishkin, DeRuiter, game designer Nicolas Kraj, lead programmer Miriam Cabrera and art director Francesco Mazza) plus about 10 contractors.

In the studio’s description on Steam, players forage for ingredients in the “forbidden wilds” outside town, battling explosive tomatoes, chaotic zucchini and vendetta-driven poultry. They then cook dishes back at the restaurant before a tyrannical mayor known as the Sindaco can shut it down. The game mixes combat and stealth with cooking mini-games based on real-world recipes.

The trailer is set to “’O surdato ’nnammurato,” a classic Neapolitan song performed by professional musicians recruited by the studio’s music director. Fishkin said he and DeRuiter both cried the first time they heard it.

Fishkin is best known in Seattle tech circles as co-founder of SEO software company Moz and audience research startup SparkToro, and he more recently launched Alertmouse, a tool for tracking online mentions. DeRuiter, a writer and author, is Snackbar’s head writer.

In a LinkedIn post this week, Fishkin recalled telling DeRuiter during the COVID lockdown that he wanted to fulfill a childhood dream of making a video game. Her reply: “Don’t wait. Do it now. I’ll do it with you.”

In the same post, he said the game’s themes include found family and fighting fascism “even when there’s no hope you’ll win.” He called it a love letter to DeRuiter’s small family village in the mountains outside Naples, to that era of Italy, to video games, and to the many people both of their families have lost in recent years.

Moments like hearing that song come often in the work, Fishkin said, such as when a new feature clicks or a new animation brings DeRuiter’s characters to life. He has always loved art without being good at any form of it. “I may not be able to create art, but I can enable it,” he said. “What a wonderful feeling.”

There have been lows, too. The team spent its initial 18 months on the project with a contract agency that didn’t work out, losing money with nothing to show for it. Fishkin is glad they kept going, “even when it felt financially irresponsible.”

The game is entirely human-made, and Snackbar’s no-AI stance is firm. “Geraldine hates AI with the fury of a thousand suns,” Fishkin said. He once suggested, just once, that she use Google’s AI Mode to find a synonym, and she was mad at him for the rest of a six-hour flight home from Philadelphia. Even if players, the rest of the team and the games media were fine with AI (and they’re not), DeRuiter alone would make it a no-go, he said.

Still ahead are 10 to 12 months of finishing the game’s content, playtesting, bug fixing, marketing and launch prep. Fishkin called it daunting, but said team members have done it many times before, “even though it’s our first rodeo.”

Fishkin is still juggling Snackbar with SparkToro and Alertmouse, and describes his role at the studio as mostly oversight and management. SparkToro is growing again, and Alertmouse recently hit a big milestone in annual renewals with high retention. He and his Alertmouse co-founders are putting more money into the company to fund growth.

Balancing the three roles is a challenge, he said, but only rarely completely overwhelming. “Like this week.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5413. NYC is spending $70 million on 5 city-run grocery stores that will price essentials 30% below retail — and bodegas are fighting back

New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.

Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.

Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers, supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses.

As a food policy scholar, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.

The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government. In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food.

It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.

That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly.

If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.

New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all.

While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices.

In this respect, the stores offer a “public option” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives, like public schools and city hospitals.

Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.

At his May announcement, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.”

Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses.

In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business.

A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods.

These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them.

FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers.

Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.

This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare.

This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “the submerged state.”

Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways.

First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food.

If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.

Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable.

To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business.

Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses.

The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.

Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.

Nevin Cohen, Chair of the Department of Health Policy and Management, CUNY Graduate School of Public Health and Public Policy
