#5412. 15 Years Ago, a Family Celebration Helped Two Sisters Notice a Gap in the Beauty Industry. Here’s How the Moment Sparked a 7-Figure Business.

Blushington co-CEOs Stephi Cohen and Nicki Maron reveal how they turned a standalone store into a growing franchise.

Fifteen years ago, Stephi Cohen and Nicki Maron encountered a common problem. The two sisters were getting ready for a special event, their younger sister’s bat mitzvah, and their family had all come over. Their house was packed, and they couldn’t afford to have a makeup artist and hair stylist cater to everyone.

“We started to think, well, you can go to Drybar and get your hair done,” Cohen says in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “But where can we go to get our makeup done?”

That’s where their “aha” moment happened. They thought that there should be a makeup place similar to Drybar but expanded, where customers could go to get their hair, makeup and skincare done, without having to pay the high price of a professional makeup artist coming to their homes.

Cohen called the business Blushington. She was just 21 years old at the time. Maron, her older sister, was 23 years old at the time and helped behind the scenes while pursuing a television career. She eventually joined the business full-time.

Today, the sisters are co-CEOs of Blushington, a company they report has a seven-figure run rate. Getting there meant rebuilding around a franchise model after temporarily closing their doors due to the pandemic.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and concision.

Stephi, what were you doing before you started Blushington?

Stephi Cohen: I went to the University of Arizona and studied a combination of communications and retail. I studied abroad in London and graduated early because I was ready to start my career. I always loved beauty and fashion — I have three sisters, and I was the one who was especially interested in that world. So, I worked in retail, but when I graduated, I wasn’t sure exactly what I wanted to do. I knew I wanted to be my own boss.

Nicki Maron: I was working in television marketing as Bill Lawrence’s assistant on Cougar Town. Working for him taught me about the power of grassroots marketing. While Stephi was developing the idea, I was helping her behind the scenes. Eventually, I realized I was probably spending more time working with her than working for Bill, and that wasn’t right. I needed to make the jump.

Also, I was thinking about how we could introduce the business to people who regularly needed their makeup done, including actresses like Courteney Cox. I was entrepreneurial, and I saw the same need Stephi saw: People didn’t have access to quality makeup applications at an affordable price.

What did you want customers to feel when they walked in?

Maron: We watched Pretty Woman as kids, and that scene where she’s treated badly in the store stayed with us. We wanted Blushington to be the opposite of that. There wasn’t a place where different generations of women could get their makeup done and feel that the artists were really listening to them. That was a big part of what we wanted to create.

Cohen: Nicki was there from the beginning, even when she had another job. She helped with everything. Having someone I trusted so much made a huge difference.

Where did the name Blushington come from?

Cohen: I had just come back from studying abroad in London. I liked names like Lexington and Kensington, but other names I considered were already trademarked. I wanted something that felt international, even though it was really two girls in Los Angeles. We combined “blush” with that kind of ending and came up with Blushington. Nobody had the name, so we could trademark it. Almost everybody in the family disliked it at first.

Maron: Myself included. I didn’t understand it. I give Stephi a lot of credit for trusting her instincts. If it had been up to me, we probably wouldn’t have gone with Blushington, and that would have been a mistake.

How did you find out whether other people shared your frustration?

Maron: We listened to friends and family. It wasn’t just us. It was our cousins, aunts, grandmothers and friends coming into town. There wasn’t a place that put service first in the way we wanted. The stores were modeled after our mom’s vanity. We wanted them to feel like a home away from home. We say that walking into Blushington should feel like a warm hug.

Stephi also believed makeup didn’t have to be reserved for weddings, prom or other special occasions. We launched services like Eyes Only for people who didn’t want a full face of makeup but still wanted to look and feel good.

What were the first concrete steps you took to get the business started?

Cohen: First, I asked people what they thought of the concept and tried to get their buy-in. Then I worked on a business plan. After that, we started looking for a location. I was driving down Sunset, near Drybar, and saw a “For Lease” sign. I thought, “This is a sign — I have to call.”

The space was a little bigger than we originally wanted, but it worked out well. From there, we needed architects and had to figure out the buildout. You learn as you go, and you surround yourself with people who have more experience than you do. For me, creating the space was the most exciting part. Then came finding the brands and sticking to our approach to product selection.

Cohen: We weren’t going to buy an entire product line just to carry a brand, and we still don’t. At the time, bigger brands often required you to meet a minimum or bring in the full line. We pushed back. We wanted to choose the products that made sense for our artists and customers.

Cohen: We brought together a board and a few investors who helped fund the buildout and the start of the business.

The pitch was that nobody was doing what we wanted to do. Investors could see the demand for blowout bars, and we were showing them a similar opportunity for makeup applications. Our product selection, artistry, pricing and overall model helped make the case.

Maron: You call everyone you know. You say, “This is what I’m doing. I need to find the right people to help me, and let’s do it together.”

Cohen: We talked to friends and family and kept getting the word out. Eventually, publicity helped bring people to us, rather than us always having to look for them. But in the beginning, we pounded the pavement.

How did you get your first paying customers?

Cohen: When we opened in 2011, Drybar was right next door. We had a great relationship, and people getting their hair done would come to us afterward for makeup. That helped introduce the business. We still believe in getting out into the community. Sometimes that means literally standing on the street and handing out cards. Nicki will do that herself.

Location matters, too. We want to be near complementary businesses — fitness, wellness and other places our customers already visit. Someone might finish a workout and come to us for a blowout.

Who did you imagine your typical customer would be?

Maron: The women who were in the room for our sister’s bat mitzvah. Someone like me who didn’t know much about makeup, someone like Stephi, who knew a lot, our mom and our grandmother.

I was a college soccer player. I didn’t wear makeup. Stephi would do my makeup, and our younger sister would do our hair.

That customer hasn’t really changed. She’s multigenerational. A mom comes in, and then her daughter comes in.

Cohen: We wanted to change the idea that getting your makeup done was only for a special occasion.

I had very bad acne in high school, and I understood what makeup could do for my confidence. I wanted to bring that experience to our customers.

It could be for a date, or it could simply be because you want to feel good about yourself. Keeping services affordable makes it easier for customers to come in more often, rather than only for a big event.

Maron: That remains part of our approach. You can get hair and makeup done under one roof for less than $200.

Maron: We signed a flagship space in New York City on March 11. On March 13, we closed our doors. It was one of the worst days of our lives. We had spent years building this family business, putting our hearts into it. We had to close all our locations and let our team go. Then we had to ask ourselves whether we should keep going at all.

Cohen: Not being able to provide income for our employees was one of the hardest parts. Before we could even figure out what we were going to do, we were worrying about them. We had to decide: Do we close the business, or can we come out of this stronger? Ultimately, we felt the franchise model was the best model for us.

Maron: During the pandemic, we created an online Blushington Academy. We certified artists across more than 40 states, and we have more than 250 artists in our portal. We wanted to support artists when people weren’t getting their hair and makeup done and we also saw more people wanting to become their own bosses. Franchising made sense because Stephi and I live in Los Angeles. Someone who lives in another city knows that community better than we do.

Maron: We have one corporate location in New York City and two open franchise locations in Boca Raton and Houston. Both franchisees were customers first. Karen, our first franchisee, had visited our Dallas and New York locations. Courtney, our Houston franchisee, had been emailing us about franchising since 2015.

Why would someone choose a Blushington franchise instead of starting an independent business?

Maron: Running a business on your own is difficult. In a franchise system, you have support. Our franchisees have Stephi, me and our team. We can help with real estate selection, marketing and operations because we’ve spent years learning how those things work. We also believe in the combination of blowouts, makeup and skincare in one appointment. Customers save time, and franchisees are working with an established concept and brand.

What affects the cost of opening a location?

Cohen: The investment includes the buildout, inventory and the products we select. We offer incentives for veterans and multi-unit owners. Our lounges also aren’t just service spaces. We host private parties and rent out the space, so that influences how we design and build them.

What did you need to demonstrate before asking someone to invest in a franchise?

Maron: We needed to show that customers wanted multiple services under one roof. We’re seeing close to two services per appointment. Someone comes in for a blowout and adds makeup or lashes. People don’t want appointments in different locations, long waits, inconsistent quality or an overwhelming product selection. Our business is built around making that easier.

#5411. Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:31 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 2:31 pm

Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension.

The condition causes high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs. It forces the heart to work harder and can lead to heart failure.

The Small Business Innovation Research fast-track award supports Lila’s efforts to develop a protein-based treatment for pulmonary hypertension that could be given by injection a few times a year.

“Most approved therapies only manage symptoms, such as vasodilators,” Lila CEO Jake Kraft said in a LinkedIn post, referring to drugs that widen blood vessels. “Lila Bio is pursuing clinically-validated, disease-modifying mechanisms that treat the underlying disease.”

The funding comes from the NIH’s National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is divided into two phases. The initial $605,981 will support early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates. The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will support further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients.

Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023. Both worked as postdoctoral fellows at UW’s Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. Lila raised $10 million in seed funding the year it was founded. Last year, it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop treatments for solid tumors.

The startup uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins through two platforms. One supports the pulmonary hypertension project, creating long-acting injectable drugs designed to remain active in the body for weeks or months. The other focuses on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to deliver radioactive isotopes to tumors.

“We want to bring medicines to patients,” Kraft told GeekWire in an earlier interview. “We don’t want to just say we’ve designed a protein, but we actually want to be able to say we’ve saved lives.”

#5410. From Gen X to Gen Z, ‘unicorn game’ GTA VI’s multigenerational pull is a threat to Hollywood’s holiday blockbusters

Thirteen years after its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto VI finally arrives on Nov. 19. The sixth installment in Rockstar Games’ open-world crime series launches on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, and its pull is likely to be felt well beyond gaming, wherever other entertainment competes for the same audience’s time.

When Grand Theft Auto V came out in 2013, it generated $800 million in sales in its first 24 hours. It has since sold nearly 235 million units, according to parent company Take-Two Interactive’s latest earnings release.

The new game is on pace to crush those numbers. Sensor Tower estimates GTA VI had logged about 12.1 million digital preorders worth roughly $1.18 billion as of the morning of Nov. 13.

If it were a movie, GTA VI would already be one of the year’s top-grossing films. Its preorders alone top the roughly $1.01 billion that The Super Mario Galaxy Movie has grossed worldwide, according to The Numbers’ 2026 worldwide box office chart.

The stakes for Take-Two are enormous. Analysts estimate the publisher has spent $1 billion to $1.5 billion on the game, as Fortune has reported on CEO Strauss Zelnick’s bet. Earlier this month, Take-Two held its forecast of $8 billion to $8.2 billion in net bookings for the fiscal year ending in March, saying preorders were running well ahead of its expectations.

Fans are clearing their calendars. In a survey of nearly 1,500 users by digital marketplace G2A.com, 29% said they had already requested time off from work or school to play the game. G2A also says its preorders surged 152% week over week in the most recent seven days.

That kind of planned absence has fueled viral estimates of what GTA VI will cost the U.S. economy, though economists told Fortune those fears are overblown.

G2A founder Bartosz Skwarczek tells Fortune, “GTA VI is much more than a game launch. It’s a global cultural moment that shows just how deeply gaming has become part of people’s lives.”

Zelnick has called GTA VI the “most anticipated entertainment property of all time,” and the rest of the industry seems to agree. Publishers have largely moved their releases out of its way, leaving this quarter unusually quiet.

“This Fall has been the most depressed Fall we’ve ever seen in terms of game volume,” Colan Neese, senior vice president of gaming at research firm Screen Engine/ASI, tells Fortune. “Basically every game that was going to come out this Fall tried to release in September and then it just fell off a cliff in October.”

The only other major releases this month look like counterprogramming. Blizzard launched World of Warcraft: Forever on Nov. 4, and Nintendo released its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 on Nov. 5.

The former is a PC and Mac game, platforms GTA VI won’t reach at launch. The latter is family-friendly and sells to a different crowd than GTA does.

GTA VI’s shadow could stretch into the new year. “It’s going to be really hard for a game to break through in December,” says Neese. “And then the question goes, how long does that shadow last? Does it go into January? Does it go into February?”

Neese points to Sony, which pushed God of War Laufey from Feb. 16 to May 20, 2027, a move he reads as steering clear of GTA VI. Sony’s Santa Monica Studio said the extra time would go toward “putting in the finishing touches.”

Hollywood may feel the squeeze, too. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens Nov. 20, the day after GTA VI, in what Fortune has called a thin November box office that GTA VI is set to test. In December, Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three both open on the 18th, each vying to be the entertainment event of the year.

Little do they know that their greatest competitor might be a video game with a vast, multigenerational audience.

“Grand Theft Auto VI is a unicorn game because it’s reaching elder millennials and young Gen Xers who grew up on Grand Theft Auto III through Grand Theft Auto V. It was a decade where they released multiple Grand Theft Autos and we all grew up with the game, played it constantly, and then it culminated with GTA V, and then it just went away when we went into our thirties.

“Now, we’re in our forties and all of a sudden, we have a new Grand Theft Auto and we’re all excited to ride the nostalgia,” explains Neese.

“Then you have an entire generation who only had one Grand Theft Auto game, which is Gen Z,” Neese continues. “They grew up with Grand Theft Auto V streamer culture on Twitch and YouTube. They had Grand Theft Auto V and then Grand Theft Auto Online, which has also brought in early Gen Alpha.

“So, you have this really interesting moment where multiple generations are just going to be sucked into this thing.”

Rockstar has a track record that justifies the anticipation. Between GTA V and VI, the studio released Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018, which has shipped more than 89 million units and remains one of the best-selling games of all time.

GTA VI itself was delayed twice, first from fall 2025 to May 2026 and then to Nov. 19, giving Rockstar more time to polish what Neese sees as a landmark.

“They purposely built a new engine. They’ve made it incredibly realistic,” says Neese. “They did a lot of research into the Southern Florida setting and culture and tried to bring this world to life.

“They put a lot of research, time, and technology into making this and it’s the pinnacle of game creation for humans. It’s like the Sistine Chapel or the Notre-Dame of what a game can be made by humans, and candidly, I don’t know if we’ll ever see the likes of this again.”

Former Take-Two CEO Ben Feder made a similar case in Fortune this week, arguing that GTA VI will be the last pre-AI blockbuster video game of its kind.

If 2013 doesn’t seem like that long ago, consider that the gap between then and now is longer than the stretch between the first and last Harry Potter movies, or between Star Wars: Revenge of the Sith and The Force Awakens. It’s also longer than the full runs of era-defining shows like Game of Thrones, Breaking Bad, The Office, Friends, and Seinfeld.

Meanwhile, the gaming industry has boomed. Americans spent $60.7 billion on video games in 2025, according to the Entertainment Software Association’s 2026 Essential Facts report, nearly triple the roughly $21 billion they spent in 2013.

The same report counts 212.3 million Americans who play video games, about two-thirds of the population. By comparison, 53% of U.S. adults told the Pew Research Center in 2025 that they had seen a movie in a theater in the past year.

Mainstream entertainment companies seem to be waking up to gaming’s potential as its core audience comes of age. Earlier attempts to adapt video games for the big screen were poorly received, but this year The Super Mario Galaxy Movie has grossed more than $1 billion worldwide and Resident Evil about $410 million.

TV series such as The Last of Us, Arcane, and Fallout have proved successful, too.

“Part of the challenge with gaming adaptations for the longest time was that you had a generation of people who never actually played or experienced the IP. Now, they have a relationship to it,” concludes Neese.

If traditionalist attitudes still siphon video games into a niche corner of the entertainment industry, Nov. 19 may be a referendum on that outlook. GTA VI stands to show how much a single game can disrupt the broader entertainment business and hold an audience’s attention for months at a time.

#5408. AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:56 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 3:19 pm

WellSaid, the AI voice company that spun out of Seattle’s Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, is reinventing itself for the era of AI agents.

The company this week launched WellSaid Producer, which connects its voiceover direction tools directly to AI assistants such as Claude and Microsoft Copilot.

Instead of logging into WellSaid’s app, corporate users can ask the AI assistant for a voiceover to accompany a training or marketing video, for example. The assistant then sends the script to WellSaid, which generates the audio using its licensed voices.

It’s part of a broader overhaul and refocusing of WellSaid’s business. The company has spent the past two years moving away from individual users to focus on businesses. It now has about 30 employees, down from more than 70 in late 2024.

Along the way, WellSaid has turned profitable, CEO Benjamin Dorr told GeekWire.

“We’ve been calling this adventure Act II, so I guess Producer is Scene I,” Dorr said. Extending the metaphor, he acknowledged that “the cast is a lot smaller,” and noted that many of the company’s leaders are new, recruited from his own network.

Dorr joined WellSaid as CFO in 2024 and became CEO in spring 2025. He was previously chief operating officer of Cordial, a San Diego marketing software company, and earlier worked in tech investing and banking at The Carlyle Group, Morgan Stanley and Citi.

He succeeded Brian Cook, the former Nintex CEO who led WellSaid for about 16 months. Co-founder Matt Hocking, who was CEO until early 2024, remains on WellSaid’s board and is now chief product officer at Type, an AI startup for creative writers.

Dorr’s leadership team includes three executives who also worked at Cordial and joined WellSaid since last fall: Natalia Holts, senior vice president of finance and accounting; Jeni Bishop, vice president of marketing; and Bryan Keefer, vice president of product.

Chris Johnson, the chief product and technology officer, and co-founder Mixail Petrochuk, the chief technology officer, remain from the earlier leadership team.

The company is maintaining its longstanding practice of building its AI voices from recordings of professional voice actors, who are paid royalties when businesses use their voices to narrate training courses, marketing and other videos.

WellSaid drew widespread attention in 2023 when it created a spot-on synthetic version of former NPR “Planet Money” host Robert Smith’s voice, with his permission, as part of a special series by the popular radio show and podcast.

Its customers include nearly half of the Fortune 100, according to WellSaid. The company’s licensing approach stands out in a sector that remains a wild west, with models trained on audio scraped from the internet and tools used to fake the voices of public figures.

“We view [Model Context Protocol], and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago.”

How it works: Producer uses Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a standard way for AI assistants to connect to other software. It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Atlassian’s Rovo, and Dorr said AI agents that work on their own will be able to use it by the end of the year.

Companies using WellSaid Producer can set up style guides so brand names, acronyms and technical terms are pronounced the same way in every file. When a product name or script changes, Producer can update every affected voiceover in one pass, and each finished file carries a record of its license.

WellSaid also says it’s the first voiceover platform to generate audio natively at 48 kHz, the standard for film and video. WellSaid will continue to offer its Studio app for customers who want to work there directly.

Producer is sold as a platform, with customers committing to buy credits for minutes of finished, licensed audio. WellSaid’s licenses today are mostly one-time buyouts, but Dorr said the company wants to price more like the traditional voiceover industry, where an ad voiceover is priced by its length, reach and how long it runs.

The strategy: Dorr said voiceover is just one step in a larger production process, and many creative tools now include basic AI speech that is sometimes good enough. He sees AI agents letting companies combine specialized tools from vendors they trust, instead of settling for one all-in-one app.

“We view MCP, and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago,” he said.

Voice actors: Actors’ revenue share rates won’t change when their voices are used through AI assistants, Dorr said. One of his first moves as CEO was to open the company’s stock option pool to its top 20 voice actors, and WellSaid is building a voice actor advisory board, with more details expected to be released in December. Dorr said WellSaid plans to add custom royalty structures, “potentially all the way up to union rate cards.”

Customers will also be able to use voice models from other companies alongside WellSaid’s own, for features its models lack, such as one voice speaking several languages. The voices still come from WellSaid’s actors under its licensing terms. “We’re not moving from our position on commercial licensing,” Dorr said.

The business: WellSaid has about 1,000 business customers, and its top 25 customers each spend more than $100,000 a year, Dorr said. Moving away from individual users “did flatten our growth compared to a lot of AI companies growing at astronomical rates,” he said.

By comparison, rival ElevenLabs, which has offered voice generation through Claude since 2025, was valued at $22 billion in a recent employee tender offer.

WellSaid raised venture debt from Multiplier Capital in March but didn’t disclose the amount. Its most recent disclosed equity funding was a $10 million Series A round in 2021 that valued the company at $65 million, according to PitchBook.

Dorr said debt was a better fit than equity for a “modestly growing and, now, profitable company,” at a time when investors’ growth expectations “have become extreme.” He said WellSaid will consider other financing in 2027 “if our ambitions outstrip our ability to reinvest.”

#5407. When Walmart pulls out of town, the stores next door don’t pick up its shoppers — their sales are down 20% a year later

Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate.

Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road.

But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger?

We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026.

This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor.

Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business.

Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect: Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants.

Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop. But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest. What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes.

A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area.

This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough.

We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open.

We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes.

That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared.

In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally.

Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand.

Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales.

Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed.

These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure.

A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores.

That creates what economists call an externality – a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits.

For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s.

Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area.

Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself – whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic.

Vivek Astvansh, Associate Professor of Quantitative Marketing and Computational Data Science, Binghamton University, State University of New York; Preetinder Kaur, Assistant Professor of Marketing, University of Guelph, and Pushpinder Gill, Assistant Professor of Marketing, Toronto Metropolitan University

#5406. This NFL Quarterback Used to Work With NASA. It Inspired Him to Change How Athletes Travel.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Lions quarterback and former NASA intern Josh Dobbs wants to redesign how pro athletes fly.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Sports were Detroit Lions backup quarterback Josh Dobbs’ first love. He started playing baseball at 4 years old, then football a year later. Those passions stuck with him as he got older, but another interest began to take shape.

“When we would travel as a family, I enjoyed going on trips that required us to fly somewhere because I liked going to the airport and seeing airplanes take off and land,” Dobbs shares. “I was fascinated by how these massive tubes of metal are flying across the country.”

Now a 10-year NFL veteran, Dobbs is exploring a future in the other field he’s passionate about: aviation and aerospace.

“I want to build an aviation infrastructure that significantly improves the way athletes travel,” Dobbs tells Entrepreneur. And based on what he’s done so far, the quarterback known as “The Passtronaut” is already well on his way.

Dobbs attended the University of Tennessee, where he threw for more than 7,000 yards, rushed for over 2,000, and accounted for 85 total touchdowns. But unlike some athletes who view college primarily as a stepping stone to the pros, Dobbs wanted to pursue a field he was genuinely passionate about while giving himself options beyond football in case his playing career didn’t work out.

That’s where aerospace engineering came in. “It was the perfect mix of aviation, but also problem-solving, math, and science, which are things I was good at in school,” Dobbs says.

He also ties it back to football, citing the work ethic and processing skills required to succeed in each field (no pun intended).

“In engineering class, they’re giving you a problem, they’re giving you equations, you’ve got to solve them, go through that thought process, apply it, and repeat the process,” Dobbs explains.

“In football, it’s the same thing. A defense will give you various coverages that you have to attack for the game. Throughout the week, you’re generating solutions to the issues that they’re giving you, and you have to go out and execute a game plan.”

He believes the methodical approach to problem-solving required of a quarterback helped prepare him for a career in engineering, and vice versa.

Dobbs’ collegiate performance earned him a spot in the NFL, where the Pittsburgh Steelers selected him in the fourth round. While he was laser-focused on establishing himself as a successful quarterback, making it to the pros didn’t mean putting his passion for aviation and aerospace on the back burner.

“You get to the NFL, and you realize outside of the season how much truly free time you have,” Dobbs shares. “My goal is always to maximize my time and opportunity.”

He didn’t have to look far for an opportunity. During Dobbs’ rookie year, he was introduced to the NFLPA Externship Program, a career-development initiative run by the NFL Players Association’s Player Affairs department. The program connects active and transitioning players with real-world work experience, networking, and mentorship outside of football. One opportunity involved Fanatics, where players traveled to different company sites across the country to get a behind-the-scenes look at the sports merchandising business.

Dobbs was impressed by the experience but wanted to apply the same concept to an industry closer to his own interests.

“I kind of wanted to take that same thought process and get a behind-the-scenes look at how one of the top engineering companies, per se, in the world works,” he says. “And so I had some contacts at NASA and was able to put together an opportunity to do a similar deal with NASA at the Kennedy Space Center.”

Dobbs spent a month at the center, shadowing engineers across different NASA departments to better understand the aerospace industry. At the time, the agency was preparing the Artemis I rocket, an uncrewed test flight designed to lay the groundwork for humanity’s return to the Moon. Dobbs joined the instrumentation group responsible for the rocket’s mobile launcher, getting a hands-on look at how engineers developed and installed the equipment used to monitor the rocket.

His second assignment brought him even closer to the action. Dobbs worked with a team developing a lunar rover designed to mine regolith, or moon dirt. Although the rover has yet to launch, he researched potential commercial rockets that could carry it to the Moon.

“That was pretty unique because I really got to see a mission, a goal, an objective, and how I could fit in and create a solution for them,” Dobbs says.

Beyond the engineering work, he also got an inside look at the business of space exploration, learning how commercial space contracts worked and about companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin. It was Dobbs’ first real exposure to the aerospace industry, and the experience only deepened his interest in the field.

“There’s a lot of emerging opportunities in commercial space,” Dobbs explains, citing tourism, scientific research, and resource storage as a few. “But I would say that experience really drew my interest back to aviation.”

In college, he had interned with Pratt & Whitney, a major aerospace manufacturer specializing in aircraft engines and other propulsion systems. Later, while playing for the San Francisco 49ers, he earned his pilot’s license, choosing the Bay Area as his classroom.

“When I was talking with other people who had gone along the path of getting their pilot license, they said the best place to fly is the Bay Area, San Francisco. It’s beautiful, a lot of air traffic, a lot of nuance. It’s very hectic, but it’s a beautiful place to fly and a great place to learn,” Dobbs says.

After his experience at NASA, Dobbs was more motivated than ever to make his mark on the aviation industry.

“My goal is to create a charter option that improves team travel,” Dobbs shares. “I think the way that sports teams travel is very unique because it’s a logistical challenge. You’re transporting anywhere from 45 to 150 large human beings across the country so they can compete at the highest level. And right now, a lot of those solutions are based on the same commercial solutions that aren’t always adequate for the customers traveling, to say the least.”

Dobbs is uniquely positioned to speak from experience, having played 10 seasons in the NFL, during which he’s flown more than the average person does in their lifetime. He believes there’s a disconnect between how much professional teams invest in player health and how little attention they pay to travel conditions.

“When you’re spending millions of dollars on your athletes, not only from a salary standpoint, but also through investments in food, nutrition, training facilities and technologies that help them rest and recover, and then you’re putting them on a plane with inadequate seating arrangements and seats that don’t fit them, asking them to travel across the country hours before a game, it’s very counterintuitive,” Dobbs explains. “They’re investing a lot in their athletes, but the solution, which really comes down to the aircraft and equipment available to teams, is what’s missing. That’s where I think there’s a great opportunity.”

Dobbs says he’s since gone on a “deep dive” into NFL and collegiate team travel schedules, drawing on his own experience with the 49ers.

“We travel a lot. There aren’t many West Coast games,” he shares of those seasons. “You’re spending a lot of time on planes, and you get off feeling tight before having to compete at the highest level. Then you get back on the plane, prepare for practice and do it all over again the next week.”

He believes investing in better travel technology and accommodations would help athletes arrive rested and ready to compete, ultimately improving the product fans see on the field and court.

“I think we all love the product of sport that we’re seeing, and we want to see it more. But the key is for the athletes to be rested, recovered, and ready to go wherever they are playing,” Dobbs says. “Creating an adequate solution for the collegiate and professional levels would ultimately improve the product that we’re seeing on every field and every court. The key is to make it sustainable.”

As Dobbs develops his own plans for the aviation industry, he’s also focused on getting more young athletes involved in STEM through the Extraordinary Dobbs Foundation. “I’ve been fortunate to have great connections and opportunities to get into the industry, and so my goal is to give back to the next generation of aerospace engineers and student-athletes who also want to pursue STEM careers,” he says.

Last year, the foundation brought seven aerospace engineering students from the University of Tennessee to Kennedy Space Center to witness the Artemis II launch. As the foundation grows, Dobbs hopes to organize more experiences like this with NASA, as well as Cirrus, an American aircraft manufacturer whose planes he used during flight training.

“I’ve crossed paths with a lot of people who have similar interests but don’t know where to start. It’s about giving them that introduction to the industry so they can build long and promising careers in STEM,” he says.

Dobbs hopes to play many more years in the NFL, but when the time comes to hang up his cleats, the veteran quarterback already has a game plan for what comes next.

“I think through the work I’ll do when I finish playing, I’ll create a successful solution that can become a catalyst for growing sports, especially football, around the world,” Dobbs says. “Because if you want to play games in Tokyo and Dubai, you’ve got to be able to get there.”

Sports were Detroit Lions backup quarterback Josh Dobbs’ first love. He started playing baseball at 4 years old, then football a year later. Those passions stuck with him as he got older, but another interest began to take shape.

“When we would travel as a family, I enjoyed going on trips that required us to fly somewhere because I liked going to the airport and seeing airplanes take off and land,” Dobbs shares. “I was fascinated by how these massive tubes of metal are flying across the country.”

Now a 10-year NFL veteran, Dobbs is exploring a future in the other field he’s passionate about: aviation and aerospace.

#5405. Ex-Seattle startup DeltaGen acquired by new AI company backed by Veeam co-founder

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 5:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 5:51 am

DeltaGen, an AI startup that got its start in Seattle before moving to San Francisco this year, has been acquired by Worker.ai, a new small-business software company backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev.

Worker, which launched Thursday, acquired all of DeltaGen for an undisclosed price that included a substantial cash component and equity in Worker, DeltaGen co-founder and CEO Rene Bystron told GeekWire.

Bystron joins Worker as co-founder and COO, and nine other DeltaGen employees are coming with him, including co-founders Michal Studnicka and Matus Ondreicka.

Worker, led by co-founder and CEO John Roberts, a former private equity operator based in Raleigh, N.C., is building software that lets small businesses hand off recurring work to AI agents. DeltaGen’s voice technology captures decisions made in conversations and turns them into assigned tasks.

Roberts had been a DeltaGen customer before Worker needed voice technology, Bystron said. “We could have raised another round and kept building independently, but this gave us the capital and experience to move faster with people we trusted,” he said.

Launched in 2024, DeltaGen raised a $1.2 million pre-seed round in early 2025 to build generative AI tools for financial professionals, with a focus on streamlining mergers and acquisitions. The company relocated from Seattle to San Francisco earlier this year.

“I still love Seattle and miss it like crazy,” said Bystron, who is keeping his apartment in Belltown. “But being closer to the AI founders, customers and investors in San Francisco makes a real difference at this stage. It also didn’t help that Washington has been chipping away at its tax advantage.”

Timashev, who co-founded data backup giant Veeam, is backing Worker to help small businesses such as manufacturers, service companies and family businesses grow.

“AI can now give small businesses more capacity without asking already stretched owners to work longer days,” he said in a statement. “Worker is my bet on that shift.” The size of his investment was not disclosed.

DeltaGen’s current product is an AI voice platform, which will continue as it’s integrated into Worker. DeltaGen’s AI voice platform will continue as it’s integrated into Worker, which is opening access gradually through a waitlist.

#5404. Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain."

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis."

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks."

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#5403. What I Learned Spending Thousands on Meta Ads to Launch a New Product

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I used to measure ad spend of tens of millions a month with a large team. Now I do most of that work on my own with AI, and here is what it can’t do.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

About a year ago, I was working for a global fintech headquartered in London. We had a budget of tens of millions of dollars per month to spend on marketing, so we worked with a fairly large marketing team. As director for growth, I was responsible for all sorts of technical marketing duties, including measurement, signals engineering, analytics and the measurement of performance in general.

We employed a large team of dozens of developers to do this. Now things have completely changed. I can do a lot of the things that I used to do with a team just on my own with AI. I wrote SQL code for years, but I’ve not written any SQL for over a year now. Most of my analyses are not done in dashboards, but via chatbot.

Having spent most of my career advising other people how to grow their business, I put it to work on my own product, RunInk, an app that turns your running routes into posters, and spent about $1,700 on Meta ads in the first month. Sales so far add up to around $200. I understand that there is a testing budget involved in these things. It’s not going to go immediately well. And in fact, it got more profitable once the ads had more to learn from.

There was a team of dozens of designers making different creatives, and many of them got released and tested and measured. Whereas now I can get Claude to make a ton of different ideas, and Meta’s AI can just test them.

It’s also not just a question of speed. Yes, AI’s creatives are often visually unappealing. But I’m not a designer. I can’t make nice things. I don’t know how to make nice things. But with the prompting, I can get AI to do it. I can focus on the winners and on getting lots of different variants out that I think might be useful.

Signals engineering was generally the martech job, and it was not an easy job — both for large companies like the one I worked for, which had a relative dearth of signals compared to ecommerce, and for small brands starting out. There can be a significant increase in performance by just doing this well.

Ad platforms run on machine learning, which requires lots of signals to be able to learn what type of person is interested in your product. Meta says an ad set needs about 50 optimization events a week to get out of its learning phase. However, if you’re starting out from zero, you have no one interested in your product. This is also the case if you sell few, but high-ticket items. You have relatively few people coming by, but you need to figure out who they are and somehow advertise something to them.

So what you start doing is breaking down the funnel into smaller steps. Do they land on my website? Do they create an account? In my case, do they connect their Strava account? Do they create an image? Do they export an image? Do they export various images?

Then you try to add some monetary value to all of these steps and break it down from there. And then you can slowly tune and adjust these values so that you stop paying for page views and for signups and eventually start buying purchases.

AI is a powerful tool, but it still makes mistakes. You need to double check AI, ask questions and validate everything. Not necessarily by manually redoing the numbers yourself, but by asking probing questions the way you would ask an intern.

Back when I managed a team, the way I would ensure numbers were right (or at least vaguely right) was by probing them. I’d tell my team: “Hey, that number seems high; are you sure about it?” or “That number seems off; can you double-check?”

Also, don’t forget that your AI agent often lacks the context you do. If you know that five of the last 10 purchases made on your site were you testing a new feature, tell it!

It is hard to build a product if you have no users. Once I had the first 100 or so users on the website, I surveyed the people who made posters.

I saw that there was some sort of demand, some happiness with the product itself. But 11 of the 16 who answered said the free digital file was enough for them. And the only way I made money was via printed posters!

This told me that I should offer a digital product. And it instantly became my best seller! Business success is about finding the right price point and the right product, and to do that, you need to talk to your customers.

If you’re starting out with a brand new product, be aware that it’s going to cost you a lot more than $1,000. To get this to work, you’re most likely going to have to spend more than that.

That being said, it’s a great way to get people to your product. If you want to find out more, I write about measurement and AI on my site.

About a year ago, I was working for a global fintech headquartered in London. We had a budget of tens of millions of dollars per month to spend on marketing, so we worked with a fairly large marketing team. As director for growth, I was responsible for all sorts of technical marketing duties, including measurement, signals engineering, analytics and the measurement of performance in general.

We employed a large team of dozens of developers to do this. Now things have completely changed. I can do a lot of the things that I used to do with a team just on my own with AI. I wrote SQL code for years, but I’ve not written any SQL for over a year now. Most of my analyses are not done in dashboards, but via chatbot.

Having spent most of my career advising other people how to grow their business, I put it to work on my own product, RunInk, an app that turns your running routes into posters, and spent about $1,700 on Meta ads in the first month. Sales so far add up to around $200. I understand that there is a testing budget involved in these things. It’s not going to go immediately well. And in fact, it got more profitable once the ads had more to learn from.

#5402. A warning for the new Congress: Don’t stop at ‘affordability’

Samantha Tweedy is the chief executive officer of the Black Economic Alliance (BEA) Foundation, the nation’s leading organization harnessing the collective expertise and influence of business leaders to expand work, wages, and wealth across the Black community. The polling cited in this piece was conducted by the Black Economic Alliance.

It was a night of historic wins for the candidates who understood that “affordability” was at the heart of this election. But the lesson of this election is bigger than the price of eggs and gas, and every candidate – Democrat and Republican – who won should be careful not to miss the point of what voters really want.

As Black business leaders who are experts in navigating and building economic opportunity when the system doesn’t deliver, we had a hunch “affordability” wasn’t telling the whole story. So we spent months before Election Day asking voters and confirmed we were right.

Through internal polling conducted by Workbench Strategies during July 2026 of 1,400 voters, including an oversample of 400 Black voters, and our two-way texting conversations with voters, we found that they gravitated toward a combination of solutions that provide immediate relief from rising costs and build pathways to help them get ahead. For example, nearly half of all voters chose both caps on medical and prescription costs (45 percent) and increasing wages to keep up with the cost of living (43 percent) as a top-three priority. Black voters were even more focused on higher wages, with 56 percent choosing it as a top-three priority.

And over and over again, voters in focus groups conducted by HIT Strategies said that they wanted to take control of their own economic futures and for leaders to remove barriers to opportunity.

It was easy to see leading up to the election that candidates who recognized these concerns and built agendas around addressing both affordability and economic opportunity would be rewarded at the ballot box. Now that we can sit with the results of the election, it’s clear that what voters were calling an affordability crisis is also an economic mobility crisis. And now, the newly elected Congress has only 18 months to demonstrate it understands the difference and begin to deliver on both.

Yes, lowering prices matters – but that only helps Americans get to the end of the month.

Helping Americans really get ahead will take solutions that make it possible to own a home, finance a business, compete for a contract, and turn a lifetime of work into lasting financial security for their children and grandchildren – in other words, it will take building pathways to work, wages, and wealth.

This conversation matters for more than economic reasons: our democracy is still on the line.

A growing body of research finds links between economic inequality, institutional distrust, and democratic backsliding. If elected officials fail to create meaningful pathways for far more Americans to get ahead – making sure work pays, wages rise, and wealth can be built – they should not be surprised when voters look elsewhere for answers in 2028 and beyond. Nor should they expect trust in our economy, our institutions, or our democracy to rebound on its own.

Fixing this requires a bold, affirmative economic plan – and for our leaders to realize they’re on the clock with voters to deliver. The good news is that there are solutions that address both sides of the challenge: actions that can help families manage rising costs today while expanding the pathways that help people get ahead over the long term.

Lawmakers should lower costs where families feel the greatest pressure. That means promoting competition in prescription drugs, lowering grocery costs, and expanding proven tax credits that help working families keep more of what they earn.

Leaders must also expand pathways to work, wages, and wealth by increasing access to homeownership, supporting entrepreneurship and small business growth, expanding opportunities for workers to own a piece of corporate profits, raising wages, and ensuring that economic growth reaches communities too often left behind.

Finally, leaders must restore trust that the economic rules are fair. That means increasing transparency in concentrated markets, enforcing fair competition, and ensuring tax regulations do not disproportionately reward those who accumulate wealth.

If leaders do not take immediate steps to address rising costs and make the country’s founding promise of opportunity a reality for more Black Americans, and consequently all Americans, we’ll continue in a downward spiral: lack of faith in economic opportunity causes lack of faith in democracy, which harms the whole economy.

Every leader who won in 2026 should take this warning seriously and signal to voters that they understand the mandate underpinning those wins. The clock starts now.

#5401. Seattle’s Allen Institute helps create a ‘Rosetta Stone’ for brain cells to unlock clues to disease

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 11, 2026 at 5:15 pm

A coalition of 56 institutions across nine countries is publishing groundbreaking research today on the basal ganglia — a group of brain structures that help control movement, emotions, motivation and habits. The region is linked to psychiatric and degenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and Parkinson’s disease.

The scientist have produced a biological Rosetta Stone that creates a shared system for naming and describing cells in the basal ganglia across species. The goal is to help researchers compare findings, collaborate and accelerate their understanding of this essential brain region.

“This is groundwork that is necessary to really make progress,” said Michael Hawrylycz, principal investigator with the Seattle-based Allen Institute who helped organize the consortium.

The project, called the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, or BICAN, produced a basal ganglia atlas that is publicly available for basic researchers, clinicians and others to use.

The research is being presented in a package of 26 articles in a special issue of the journal Cell. The data comes from humans, macaques, marmoset and mice. One of the benefits of comparing the basal ganglia between species is understanding which components are uniquely human, providing potential insights into neurological diseases.

Despite the critical and wide-ranging roles, the basal ganglia is relatively small — it’s about 2% of the brain with a volume roughly the size of a large gumball.

For the project, the researchers pulled information from 25.5 million brain cells, including 21 million human cells. They used a variety of techniques to tease out insights, including RNA sequencing to identify gene activity from single cells in precise locations; epigenomic studies revealing where genes are switched on or off; and measurements of electrical activity combined with cell shape and genetic information.

It’s a lot of data to stitch together and make sense of, Hawrylycz said. “AI is a perfect tool” for the job, he said, because it excels at finding patterns.

The findings could help guide future treatments, but the work remains basic research rather than clinical research, Hawrylycz said.

The new research is the first major installment of the third phase of a brain-mapping effort that began in 2014. The first phase demonstrated that scientists could analyze individual cells on a large scale. The second produced an atlas of the mouse brain.

BICAN aims to create a standardized atlas describing cells throughout the brains of humans and other primates. Hawrylycz said the work is expected to take another two or three years.

#5400. Tech Executives Tell Me What They Tell No One Else, and I Think ‘The Audacity’ Got Silicon Valley Mostly Right.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

An executive coach who hears what tech leaders say behind closed doors weighs in on how “The Audacity” gets Silicon Valley right.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

“More than physical pain, I fear humiliation.” That’s the first line of The Audacity, spoken by tech CEO Duncan Park (Billy Magnussen) to his therapist. I’ve coached tech leaders for more than a decade, including people who reported directly to Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Steve Huffman, and I can’t recall a client ever saying the word “humiliation” to me. They say “insecure” and “imposter syndrome” instead. The show names a real fear in its opening seconds, using a word I rarely hear.

The series aired on AMC this spring and landed on Netflix in August, where it’s finding a second audience.

Most of the reviews came from TV critics, but I watched it as the person executives say these things to. They tell me things they keep from their boards, their teams and their partners.

With that in mind, I wanted to share what the show gets right about the people leading the tech industry and what was stretched to make good TV.

In episode seven, Duncan says the fear of humiliation is behind every little lie. His therapist, Dr. JoAnne Felder (Sarah Goldberg), puts it another way: Everyone spins, even to themselves. That’s the most accurate line in the series.

Executives spin to me, too. It usually sounds like catastrophizing what a boss might say or fixating on the worst-case scenario of an important meeting or presentation. When I hear it, I ask them to pause and take a breath. Then we get clear on what they value and what they want. Then they pick one small step forward. It’s simple, and that’s why it works.

The pause does most of the work. Once a leader slows down, the spin falls apart on its own.

In the first episode, Duncan screams at his housekeeper for failing to catch a tungsten cube he throws to her. One recap called his outbursts one of the funniest elements of the premiere. I call it reality. I’ve coached executives whose CEOs screamed at them and berated people in executive meetings — at companies that have been voted “best place to work.”

The show also gets right the fact that founders and boards tolerate this behavior. When it’s the CEO yelling, the people in the room have few options. A senior executive I coached reported directly to a CEO like this. Our work focused on how to manage themselves long enough to get out and find a healthier environment, which they did. Sometimes the only fix is a new employer.

Carl Bardolph (Zach Galifianakis) is the billionaire Duncan wants to become. A teenager in the show describes him as worth a bazillion dollars and the saddest man you’ve ever seen. Everyone in the series has money and wants more of something else, whether it’s legacy, power, impact or control.

I hear this constantly. A client of mine had led teams through back-to-back acquisitions and an exit, and he told me it still didn’t feel like enough. I didn’t tell him he had a problem or suggest he look for happiness outside work. He brought the questions to me, and my job was to help him unpack them. He wanted to know:

He chose his career goal, C-suite roles and added conditions that had never been on the list, such as remote or hybrid work, time with his school-aged children and partner, real work-life balance and room to travel. Eventually, he landed a role on those terms.

Duncan blackmails his therapist. I’ve never been blackmailed by a client, and I’m confident that’s the norm. The jargon also runs heavier than real life. Silicon Valley loves shorthand, but “quant ben” for quantifiable benefits was new to me.

The biggest stretch comes from Ethan Stern (Patrick Gilmore), Orson’s biological father, who is back in Baltimore while his son gets shipped off to Palo Alto. He tells Orson the world there is not the real world, but Silicon Valley is the world for a lot of people. Meta alone reports 3.6 billion people using its apps on an average day. Carl also claims that every billionaire eventually decides whether to save the world or control it, and that “most of us go Dr. Evil.” In my experience, most of the leaders I work with are focused on making a positive difference. The bad ones just get more publicity.

One line made me laugh out loud, and it turned out to be accurate. In the first episode, Anushka Bhattachera-Phister (Meaghan Rath) refers to Xander, the AI her husband Martin (Simon Helberg) is building, as “a digital child.” I’ve heard a tech executive use that exact phrase. The realtor telling Dr. Felder “$2.5 mil is a steal around here” got me too, as did their portrayal of office space costing $175 an hour. That’s why I coach from my home office over Zoom.

It’s lonely at the top, and the show gets that right in every storyline. Each major character is isolated, and none of them says so out loud. Some leaders I work with run from that conversation with themselves. The ones I’ve watched make progress bring it to someone else instead, whether that’s a coach, mentor or therapist, and speak honestly about their feelings.

The Audacity packs stock fraud, blackmail, ayahuasca, a tungsten cube and a wildfire into eight hour-long episodes, and AMC renewed it for a second season before the first one even aired. I’d give it a thumbs up as a composite portrait of working in tech, two thumbs up for entertainment and a thumbs down for anyone hoping to feel better about the industry afterward. Nobody was watching it for that anyway. Remember, you’ve got this!

I’ve coached tech leaders for more than a decade, including people who reported directly to Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Steve Huffman, and I can’t recall a client ever saying the word “humiliation” to me. They say “insecure” and “imposter syndrome” instead. The show names a real fear in its opening seconds, using a word I rarely hear.

#5399. The case of Nvidia and the growing risk of AI and corruption

Susan Ariel Aaronson directs George Washington University’s Institute for International Science and Technology Policy and is co-PI of the NSF-NIST Institute for Trustworthy AI in Law and Society.

In 2025, the UN Office of Drugs and Crime and the Organization of American States co-convened a panel (slideshow & video) which examined whether AI is the biggest corruption risk in history. In November 2026, the panelists’ deepest fears about the AI-corruption relationship came true, but not in the way they expected.

The panelists feared that AI would enable corruption by making it easier to launder money, give bribes, or produce disinformation. Instead, they learned that the corruption of AI did not start inside the technology itself but with its leaders, heads of state, government officials, and tech CEOs, steering the direction of AI governance. As we see today, America’s approach to AI governance, using export controls to regulate the supply of AI and its components, is fueling corruption. We utilize Transparency International’s definition herein– the abuse of entrusted authority for private gain.

I believe that one company, Nvidia, has become the poster child for corruption in the U.S. Last year, the Trump Administration restricted sales of chips to China under U.S. law out of fears that would provide the Chinese military with an advantage or could undermine U.S. leadership in AI. The now former CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, used flattery and donations to influence the Trump Administration’s AI export policies. And in December, Mr. Trump gave Nvidia permission to sell the H200, an older but still powerful A.I. chip, to China, as long as the U.S. government was given a cut of the sales. (Another company AMD also received an exemption). In so doing, the U.S. gained a financial incentive for loosening controls of AI infrastructure to China However, the Congressional Research Service reported that .”Article I, Section 9, Clause 5 of the U.S. Constitution,prohibits the federal imposition of export taxes and duties (not user fees), and 50 U.S.C. §4815(c), which prohibits BIS from collecting fees for considering or issuing export licenses.”

Additionally, last year, Nvidia’s General Counsel, Tim Teter, seemed to interfere in an investigation of Nvidia’s sales to Chinese and Malaysian entities. And now we’ve learned that although senior administration officials such as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were warned about the dangers surrounding Nvidia and its now former CEO, they took no action. This corruption and inaction puts U.S. national security and the American people at risk.

While export controls may be useful and necessary, they are particularly vulnerable to corruption because they sit at the intersection of high-value restricted goods, bureaucratic gatekeeping, in customs, business, and trade policymaking agencies, and complex cross-border supply chains. When governments restrict access to lucrative technologies, including dual use items such as chips or AI, they can create massive financial incentives for bad actors to bribe officials or exploit regulatory blind spots to bypass the rules. Export control systems rely on government officials to issue licenses, classify goods, and clear shipments through customs. This concentration of discretionary power allows corrupt officials to solicit bribes in exchange for faster approvals or looking the other way. At the same time, U.S. agencies struggle to coordinate trade, customs, and anti-corruption efforts, which are controlled by different agencies.

Export controls also create situations of artificial scarcity and high profits, particularly for dual use items such as AI systems. Some buyers may be willing to pay extremely high prices to receive a limited supply of AI services. Not surprisingly, both competitors of Nvidia that produce high speed chips such as Google, and, as well as Open AI, Amazon, Anthropic, and Microsoft—three of Nvidia’s biggest clients—support legislation that would further limit Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China.

Finally, export controls often involve opaque national security exemptions. Because export decisions often involve classified intelligence or sensitive defense deals, licensing and procurement processes frequently lack transparency and accountability. Such situations make it difficult for independent watchdogs to spot irregularities However, the Trump Administration fired many inspector generals in 2025, including at the Department of Commerce, along with antiorruption prosecutors. .

Given these problems, export controls are not the best tool to prevent our adversaries from acquiring advanced AI systems or chips because they present many opportunities for corruption. Yet Politico has reported that it is almost impossible for members of Congress to support loosening export controls. Studies have shown such controls are rarely effective. Hence, Congress should weigh a different approach Morreover, current export control implementation can harm U.S. economic and technological competitiveness. . While there are no easy answers, , the U.S. should work with its Western allies to to manage technology transfers that might threaten our shared security interests
